newsitem.title: USA: Arduous jury selection to begin in U.S. bomb case.
newsitem.headline: Arduous jury selection to begin in U.S. bomb case.

text.p: The painstaking process of selecting an impartial jury was set to begin on Monday at the start of the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh.

In a tightly-guarded Denver courthouse, U.S. District Judge Richard Matsch, prosecutors and defence attorneys were expected to closely question prospective jurors about their views and knowledge of the highly-publicised case.

McVeigh, 28, a Gulf War veteran, is charged with detonating a huge fertiliser and fuel oil truck bomb outside the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people and injuring more than 500 others. Among the dead were 19 children.
The attack, the deadliest on U.S. soil, smashed the sense of security of middle America and has permanently scarred the people of Oklahoma City.

McVeigh and former army buddy Terry Nichols, who prosecutors say shared strong anti-government views, are accused of carrying out the attack in revenge for the federal raid on the Branch Davidian sect's compound in Waco, Texas that caused about 80 deaths on April 19, 1993 -- exactly two years before the Oklahoma City blast. Both men have pleaded not guilty. Nichols will be tried later.

Oklahoma Gov. Frank Keating, who tried to reassure shocked Oklahoma City residents in the days after the blast, said on Sunday he hoped the "truth will come out" during the trial, expected to last up to four months.

"Oklahoma has no interest in convicting innocent people. Because of the horrific nature of this event we want the right people identified, the right people tried, convicted and executed. We hope these are the people," the Republican governor said on NBC's "Meet the Press".

The trial was moved to Denver because of concerns that McVeigh could not get a fair trial in Oklahoma City. The Denver courthouse has been turned into a fortress, with concrete barriers placed all around the building, security cameras scanning the sidewalks and metal detectors at the doors.

At Judge Matsch's request, the recently-remodeled courtroom being used for the trial includes none of the traditional trappings of a federal courtroom such as the Seal of the United States, The Denver Post said. It said Matsch wanted to eliminate the symbols to avoid any visible reference to the federal offices destroyed in the Oklahoma City bombing.
Twelve seats for victims have been set aside in court. Other victims and relatives will watch proceedings in Oklahoma City on closed-circuit television.
The first task is to select 12 jurors and six alternates, a process expected to take several weeks.

Summonses were originally sent to 1,000 residents of Denver and 22 surrounding counties -- the largest jury pool in Colorado history -- and 500 of those have completed a confidential questionnaire about their opinions that they will be asked more closely about in court.
Both prosecutors and defence attorneys will seek to eliminate potential jurors who appear hostile to their case.

Legal experts say the bombing has been so highly publicised that it will be virtually impossible to find jurors who know nothing about the case, but defence attorneys will try to avoid having jurors on the panel who have been exposed to negative pre-trial publicity about McVeigh.

McVeigh's lawyers have complained that prospective jurors will be prejudiced against him because of recent news reports -- denied by lead defence attorney Stephen Jones -- that McVeigh confessed to his lawyers that he was responsible for the bombing.
But a federal appeals court on Friday rejected Jones' attempts, on publicity and other grounds, to have the trial postponed.

Once the evidence phase of the trial begins, legal experts predict that prosecutors will base their case against McVeigh on extensive physical evidence as well as records and witnesses to show he rented the truck used in the bombing.
McVeigh's lawyers say he is innocent. They have suggested that a foreign country, probably Iraq, may have planned the attack, recruiting American neo-Nazis to carry out the bombing.
